description_full: Baker Hughes Company provides a portfolio of technologies and services to energy and industrial value chain. Its Oilfield Services & Equipment segment designs and manufactures exploration, appraisal, development, production, rejuvenation, and decommissioning products and related services for onshore and offshore oilfield operations. This segment also provides drilling services, drill bits, and drilling and completions fluids; completions, intervention, measurements, pressure pumping, and wireline services; artificial lift systems, and oilfield and industrial chemicals; subsea projects and services, flexible pipe systems, and surface pressure control systems; and integrated well services and solutions. It serves oil and natural gas companies; the United States and international independent oil and natural gas companies; national or state-owned oil companies; engineering, procurement, and construction contractors; geothermal companies; and other oilfield service companies. The company's Industrial & Energy Technology segment offers gas technology equipment, such as drivers, driven equipment, and turnkey solutions for the mechanical and electric-drive, compression, and power-generation applications; aftermarket support and uptime gas technology services; non-destructive testing technologies, software, and services; pre-commissioning and maintenance services; flow control and safety solutions; mechanical and electromechanical gear transmission systems; Cordant, a software solution to optimize assets, processes, and energy use; Bently Nevada, a sensing and protection hardware for rack-based vibrating monitoring equipment and sensors; and climate technology solutions. It serves industrial, upstream, midstream, downstream, onshore, offshore, and small-to-large scale customers. The company was formerly known as Baker Hughes, a GE company and changed its name to Baker Hughes Company in October 2019. The company was incorporated in 2016 and is based in Houston, Texas.

financial_summary: Baker Hughes Company is a large-cap energy business with a $49.1B market cap on $27.7B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +9% over the past three years, a respectable pace for a business of this size.

Returns on capital run at 8% against a 8% cost of capital, which means the business is destroying value with every dollar it reinvests, and 19% gross margins are typical of commodity economics where competitors can replicate the product cheaply.

The business throws off $2.5B in free cash flow — roughly 9 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.47× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, leverage is comfortably conservative at 1.5× net debt/EBITDA, and interest coverage runs at 9.8×.

Shareholder yield of 2.6% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome.

sect: Its 10% operating margin trails the Energy median (16%) by 5pp, so it is a below-average operator in its field.
It earns less of the sector's profit than its revenue share would suggest (0.95x).
It accounts for 0.7% of sector revenue and 0.7% of sector operating profit.
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.05 across 203 companies in the universe; the top four hold 40% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a strong uptrend, up 20% over the past year excluding the latest month, though it has pulled back 23% over the last three months.
The price sits near the bottom of its 52-week range, 30% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 35% and a beta of 0.78, it is more defensive than the market.
Liquidity is deep, with about $407.3M traded a day.
In past sell-offs it fell 63% in the 2020 crash, 47% in the 2022 bear market and 71% in 2008.
val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $24.57 (margin of safety -101%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 24%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $19.41 to $31.56 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks expensive against Energy peers: P/E 17.0 vs 13.6, EV/EBITDA 12.3 vs 7.1 and P/FCF 19.4 vs 14.6 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 3% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are mixed: an FCF yield of 5.2% (above the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 4.7% (vs the 8% bar).
The 24 covering analysts target $70.00 on average, 42% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 8% falls short of the cost of capital of 8.2%, so growth at these returns destroys value.
It runs a 19% gross margin and converts 9% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 1.47x.
ROE of 14% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (2.2x equity multiplier).
Operating margin is running 13pp above its own historical average, a peak-margin risk if conditions normalise.
It spends 2.2% of revenue on R&D and 0.7% on stock compensation.
hlth: Leverage is conservative at 1.5x net debt to EBITDA ($5.4B of cash against $6.1B of debt), with interest covered 9.8x.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 9.4% over 3 years and 6.0% over 5 years, so growth is accelerating, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 13%).
At current returns, reinvesting 31% of profits supports about 2.5% a year of fundamental growth, too little to drive meaningful growth.
Free cash flow has compounded 50.4% a year over five years.
Forward indicators: a book-to-bill of 1.10 (orders outpacing sales), a backlog worth 1.3x annual revenue and deferred revenue up 4%.
Capex roughly matches depreciation (1.1x, 4.6% of sales), a maintenance pace.
own: Insiders hold little stock (0.2%), and institutions hold 98%.
Insider trading is two-way: 1 purchase and 10 sales over the past year, net $47.8M sold.
It returns 2.6% a year to shareholders (0.8% in buybacks and 1.9% in dividends).
It has paid a dividend for 38 consecutive years, raising it 13.3% a year over the last five.
